source_text: Si dixeris, nomine concupiscentiae, etiam illum ipsum modum, quo licita rerum naturalium afficitur voluptate, ut concupiscentia carnis in universum reprobata videatur; ergo et sensum oculorum, et mundum ipsum, et quidquid in mundo est, a diabolo conditum profitere; quia omnia pariter ex Deo non esse dicuntur. Quod certe si annueris, non efficieris Manichaeus; es enim etiam nunc; sed hoc te esse, ut argumentis tuis olim, ita quoque professione monstrabis. Si autem nudatum errorem pavescens, dixeris Apostolum nomine concupiscentiae carnis et oculorum concupiscentiae, et nomine mundi, non res ipsas, quae cum intra concessos fines tenentur, innocuae sunt; cum autem in illicita procurrunt, fiunt reprehensibiles, adnotasse; clarebit, quod in primo opere egimus, concupiscentiae naturalis non genus, non speciem, non modum, sed excessum tantum in culpam venire. Atque ideo hoc testimonium Apostoli in reliquum pudenter caveto, ne illud si vel levi commemoratione pollueris, defensus quidem nihil, propalam vero proditus approberis.
pass_a_gloss: If you shall have said that by the name of desire even that very measure is meant by which one is affected with permitted pleasure of natural things, so that the desire of the flesh seems reprobated in the universe; therefore profess also that the sense of the eyes, and the world itself, and whatever is in the world, was founded by the devil; because all things equally are said not to be from God. Which certainly if you shall have granted, you will not be made a Manichaean; for you are one even now; but you will show that you are this, as formerly by your arguments, so also by profession. But if, fearing a stripped error, you shall have said that the Apostle by the name of the desire of the flesh and of the desire of the eyes, and by the name of the world, marked not the things themselves, which when they are held within granted bounds are harmless, but when they run forward into illicit things become blameworthy; it will be clear, what we did in the first work, that not the genus, not the species, not the measure of natural desire, but only the excess comes into fault. And therefore for the future beware this testimony of the Apostle modestly, lest if you pollute it even by a light commemoration, you be approved as having defended nothing indeed, but as having been openly betrayed.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: If you say that the name “desire” (1 John 2:16) includes even that measure in which it experiences the lawful pleasure of natural things, so that the desire of the flesh seems condemned in its entirety, then profess that the sense of sight, the world itself, and everything in the world were created by the devil. For all are equally said not to be from God. If you agree to that, you will certainly not become a Manichaean, since you already are one. You will simply show it by your confession, as you long ago showed it by your arguments. But if, frightened at having your error exposed, you say that under the names “desire of the flesh,” “desire of the eyes,” and “world” the apostle did not condemn the things themselves—which are harmless when they remain within permitted limits, and become blameworthy when they run into forbidden territory—then the point I argued in my first work will be clear: neither the kind, nor the form, nor the proper measure of natural desire is blameworthy, but only its excess. Therefore have the decency to leave this apostolic testimony alone from now on. If you pollute it with even a passing mention, you will be shown to have gained no defense at all, while being publicly exposed (compare 1 John 2:16).

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
